| [CASE-385](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-385.md) | Permutation-aligned MLPs and loss barriers | [LEAD-157](../../../record/leads.d/LEAD-157.md)'s design run at toy scale on CPU. Two-hidden-layer ReLU MLPs are trained in numpy on a task with two redundant cues, A and B. A test that uses no barrier says which cue each net relies on: its accuracy when only A, or only B, carries the label. Pairs are aligned four ways (none, weight matching, activation matching, and rescaling quotiented before weight matching), and at width 5 by an exhaustive search over permutations plus optimised rescaling. The barrier is then measured on the straight line, a trained Bezier curve and a trained one-bend polychain. The aligned linear barrier falls with width for every kind of pair. At width 5, three of four pairs that both rely on cue A keep a loss barrier of 0.09 to 0.25 after the exhaustive search, about as much as pairs relying on different cues (0.15 to 0.54). At widths 64 and 256 an A-net and a B-net are connected after activation matching (0.000). A copy of a net, permuted and rescaled per unit, computes exactly the same function, yet permutation alignment alone leaves it a barrier of 0.19 to 0.59. In a load-by-temperature grid, one cell is flat and poorly connected without alignment. There, alignment plus a trained curve removes the barrier, while the aligned straight line keeps 0.07 error, and the cell's accuracy deficit stays. The wording is the assistant's (Claude, in this session); adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |

In numpy (scratch/studies/lead-005/, 15 tests), 300 random 4-state systems driven by a 3-symbol Markov signal through Metropolis kernels satisfy the per-switch identity (Eq. 14), the summed identity (Eq. 17) and the heat identity (Eq. 19) to 3e-15, and the bounds (Eqs. 16, 18, 21) in every instance; no step's nostalgia is negative; Monte Carlo trajectories agree with the exact averages. With the drive made to depend on the system's state (500 systems), the identities and the summed bound still hold, but a step's nostalgia is negative in 405, the summed nostalgia in 323, and the dissipation and the excess work in 6. In an 8-percept loop where the predictive partition is a sticky nuisance and the interventional partition is the context the action must match, the memory that keeps only the context is the cheapest that does the task by every cost measured; the policy that uses it changes its nostalgia from ln 2 to 0 and leaves its heat per step unchanged. | [CASE-402](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-402.md) v2 | SGD vs the 6-gon in the toy superposition model | [LEAD-175](../../../record/leads.d/LEAD-175.md) asked for the two tests [QUESTION-363](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-363.md)'s note of 2026-11-06 moved there from [THEORY-1275](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1275.md): SGD at n = 1,000 and on both sides of n ≈ 600 across rates, batch sizes and initialisations, to see whether the 6-gon is reached; and posterior sampling across n to check the critical sample sizes the free-energy formula gives for the chain 4⁺⁺⁻ → 4⁺ → 5 → 5⁺. In the model of Chen et al. ([LIT-1894](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1894.md)), in numpy: no SGD run reached the 6-gon. The 5-gon's dropped feature gets an exactly zero gradient from every sample, so SGD cannot move it at any setting. The 5⁺-gon is a live local minimum that SGD does not leave in 45,000 epochs. Sampling exp(−nL) under the N(0, 1) prior puts 5 → 6 at n ≈ 265–279 and 5 → 5⁺ at n ≈ 780. The first two steps of the chain have no crossing above n ≈ 1. Chen et al.'s NUTS likelihood carries a factor ½ that their formula's nL does not, so their sample size is twice these n; on that scale the sampled 5 → 6 is at about 530–560, consistent with their Fig. 2. The wording is the assistant's (Claude, in this session); adopting it is the owner's call. | Active |

| [CASE-404](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-404.md) | Crossed intervention on a small network | The two interventions of [CASE-113](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-113.md), crossed, on one small network trained conventionally on two tasks with a task-identity input: a width-32 two-layer ReLU network, trained by heavy-ball SGD or by Adam, twelve seeds each. The conflicting learning demand is a change of task B's target to one opposed to task A (cosine −0.87), trained jointly; the response is how much task A is lost while B is relearned. Holding the network fixed and changing the optimizer, at matched pace, moved the response in every trained network (by −39% to +147% of the baseline loss). Holding the optimizer fixed and disrupting a learned state also moved it: re-initializing the eight most task-selective hidden units and healing raised the loss of A by 61% under the training optimizer for heavy-ball-trained networks, and eight random units did not. Neither limb of [CLAIM-367](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-367.md)'s defeat condition held. The share of the response that varies with the optimizer, against the share that varies with the learned state, depended on which optimizer had trained the network. One small network, full batch, twelve seeds. The wording is the assistant's (Claude, in this session); adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |

Over 40 seeds, readout-only training from P_c reaches the same solution for every c, while full fine-tuning does not: on a main task using 2 of the 10 pretrained dimensions, c = 0.3 beat c = 2 in 29 of 40 seeds (sign test p = 0.006); on one using all 10 with varied coefficients, c = 2 beat c = 0.3 in 40 of 40. Halving the step size moved errors by far less than these gaps. One solvable model, Gaussian inputs, numpy on CPU. The wording is the assistant's (Claude, in this session); adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |
